rows: Employers must protect workers from injury risks created by hazardous manual handling.
Hazardous manual handling should be avoided so far as reasonably practicable.
Manual-handling operations that cannot be avoided should be assessed.
Residual handling risk should be reduced to as low as reasonably practicable.
Assessment should consider the task, load, working environment and individual capability.
Handling aids and changes to layout or process can reduce physical load.
Workers need suitable information and training about the handling task and controls.
Controls should be reviewed when loads, tasks, staffing or workplace conditions change.
A stated load weight or job title does not establish the actual manual-handling risk.
Task-level conclusions require current evidence about posture, frequency, distance, grip, environment and worker capability.
Employers must protect qualifying display-screen users from health risks associated with their work.
A suitable workstation assessment is required for workers who use display-screen equipment as defined by the regulations.
Workstations should be arranged to support comfortable posture and suitable viewing.
Employers should reduce identified workstation risks rather than relying only on worker adaptation.
Work routines should include breaks or changes of activity from prolonged display-screen work.
Workers can request an eyesight test provided under the display-screen rules.
Users need information and training on workstation adjustment and safe working habits.
Assessments should be reviewed when equipment, workplace, work pattern or user needs change.
Computer ownership or time logged into software does not prove that a workstation is suitable.
Individual conclusions require current workstation, posture, duration, task, vision and adjustment evidence.
Users of pressure systems must provide equipment that is safe and suitable for its intended purpose.
Safe operating limits should be known before a pressure system is used.
Suitable protective devices should be fitted and kept functional.
Pressure equipment should be maintained through a system-level maintenance programme.
Relevant systems may require a written scheme of examination.
Examinations under the written scheme should be completed by a competent person.
Repairs and modifications should preserve the safety of the pressure system.
Operating instructions and emergency arrangements should reflect the stored-energy hazard.
A pressure rating or inspection label does not prove that a complete system is currently safe.
System conclusions require design, fluid, operating limits, protective devices, examination, maintenance and modification evidence.
Employers must identify dangerous substances that can create fire, explosion or metal-corrosion risks.
Risks from dangerous substances must be assessed.
Fire and explosion risks should be eliminated where reasonably practicable.
Where elimination is not possible, risks should be controlled and their consequences mitigated.
Employers should prepare procedures for accidents, incidents and emergencies involving dangerous substances.
Workers need information and training about substances, hazards and control measures.
Areas where explosive atmospheres may occur should be identified and classified.
Ignition sources and unsuitable equipment should be controlled in hazardous areas.
The presence of a flammable product does not establish that an explosive atmosphere exists.
Site conclusions require substance, quantity, release, ventilation, ignition, area-classification and emergency evidence.
